title: Our School Should Start Composting
passage_text:
Every day, the cafeteria at Lakeview Middle School throws away bags of fruit peels, half-eaten sandwiches, and soggy salad. Our school should start a composting program, because turning food scraps into soil would cut our trash, save money, and give students a hands-on way to learn science.

The numbers make a strong case. During a one-week audit last October, our science club weighed the cafeteria trash and found that about 60 percent of it was food waste. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, food scraps that are buried in landfills break down without oxygen and release methane, a gas that traps heat in the atmosphere.

Composting could also save the school money. The district pays a hauling company by the ton, so sending less trash to the landfill would lower that bill. A middle school in a nearby district reported cutting its trash pickups from five days a week to three after starting its own program.

Teachers support the idea as well. Ms. Alvarez, who teaches seventh-grade science, told the club that a compost bin would let students measure temperature, track decomposition, and test soil in the school garden instead of just reading about these processes in a textbook.

Some people suggest a simpler alternative: asking students to take less food so there is less to throw away. Reducing waste is a worthy goal, but students cannot control the portions that are served, and even careful eaters leave peels and cores behind. Others worry that compost bins will smell or attract pests. Well-managed bins with lids and the right mix of dry leaves rarely cause either problem.

A composting program asks little of us and gives back a great deal. The school board should approve a one-semester pilot this spring.
